doc.title: Chuck Findley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 6, 2023

title: Adapting style to artists and producers
summary: Findley says he learned to play like Sweets, Miles or Maynard, Dixieland or mariachi vibrato, by listening.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Let me ask you if you became a popular call to come in and solo as well as the section work, did you find that after you did it a lot that you might try to alter your style a bit depending on the artist or the producer?
Oh yeah. You have to make them happy.
How did you learn — you just learned from experience that Quincy Jones would like this kind of thing and Barbra Streisand would like something different?

Of course. That’s from, once again, playing all different styles and listening, you have to listen. You listen to records, listen to the radio, you’ve got to listen to what’s going on. And I listened to Sweets, like I said, you know, somebody would say well I want you to play like Sweets, I want you to play like Miles. I had it in my head. It was in there. All the motors were in there that had all that information in the computer you know? It was all in here. And I just had to pull it out and say okay, I know that, I know how to do that and I’ll do my best job sounding like him but it’s going to be me, my soul and my being like Sweets or like Conte Candoli or Snooky or Maynard whenever they had me do the Maynard or whatever I had to do I did it. But I had the knowledge from listening. And you just — once again, that’s being a soloist, you know, being like — you know if they wanted a Dixieland solo I’d play a Dixieland solo. Mariachi vibrato is different than Italian vibrato. They’re different. So if they wanted the mariachi vibrato you’d use the mariachi vibrato. If they wanted Italian vibrato, you used an Italian vibrato. They’re all different. But that you can only learn by listening. And you have to listen. And I was fortunate enough to be able to sit next and listen to them live. You can’t get that kind of schooling. That schooling is — you know what you’re doing is wonderful ‘cause you can play — at least these students can listen and get something out of it. You know like I told you before, Bobby Hackett was first. And if they haven’t listening to Bobby Hackett, they need to listen to Bobby Hackett. Bix Beiderbecke. Listen to Bix Beiderbecke. Listen to Charlie Shavers. You know? Listen to these people and listen to Pops.
